title: Why Changing One List Changed Another: Copies in Python
excerpt: Understand why assigning a list does not copy it, and how copy(), slicing and deepcopy() give you independent copies.

headings.text: When a Copy Still Shares Things
The Same Trap With Function Arguments
Do Numbers and Text Have This Problem?

html:
You make a backup of a list, change the original, and the backup changes too. Nothing in the code looks wrong, yet two variables that should be separate behave as one. This is one of the most surprising moments for new Python programmers, and it has a clear explanation.

In Python, assigning a list to a new name does not copy the list; it gives the same list a second name. This lesson shows the surprise, then the three ways to make a real copy, and where even a real copy can still fool you.

The Surprise

The method append adds an item to the end of a list. Watch what happens when two names share one list:

a = [1, 2, 3]
b = a
b.append(4)

print(a)
print(b)
[1, 2, 3, 4]
[1, 2, 3, 4]

You only changed b, so why did a change? Because b = a did not build a second list. It attached a second name to the list that already existed, so a and b are two labels on one list stored in the computer's memory. You can ask Python directly whether two names point at the same object with is:

print(a is b)
True

Make a Real Copy

To get an independent list, ask for a copy. Which of the three common ways should you use? They all behave the same, so pick the one you find most readable:

c = a.copy()
d = list(a)
e = a[:]

c.append(5)

print(a)
print(c)
print(c is a, d is a, e is a)
[1, 2, 3, 4]
[1, 2, 3, 4, 5]
False False False

The method copy(), the list() function and the full slice [:] (which means "everything from the start to the end") each build a new list holding the same items. Changing c left a alone, and all three comparisons with is are False.

When a Copy Still Shares Things

Now try a list that contains other lists. Here matrix holds two lists, [1, 2] and [3, 4]:

matrix = [[1, 2], [3, 4]]
shallow = matrix.copy()

shallow[0].append(99)

print(matrix)
print(shallow)
print(shallow[0] is matrix[0])
[[1, 2, 99], [3, 4]]
[[1, 2, 99], [3, 4]]
True

You made a copy, so why did the original change? Because the copy is only one level deep. Python built a new outer list, but the items inside it, the inner lists, were not copied. Both outer lists still hold the very same inner lists. This kind of copy is called a shallow copy.

Deep Copy for Nested Data

Do you then always need a deep copy? No, only when the list contains other changeable things. When you do need everything copied all the way down, use deepcopy() from the copy module. A module is a file of ready-made Python tools, and import loads it so you can use what is inside:

import copy

original = [[1, 2], [3, 4]]
deep = copy.deepcopy(original)

deep[1].append(55)

print(original)
print(deep)
[[1, 2], [3, 4]]
[[1, 2], [3, 4, 55]]

This time the original is untouched, because the inner lists were copied too. The name copy.deepcopy reads as "the deepcopy tool inside the copy module".

The Same Trap With Function Arguments

The sharing also happens when you pass a list to a function. A function is a named block of code you can run on demand: def creates it, the name in parentheses (items) is a placeholder for whatever you pass in, and return hands a result back to the code that called it. The list you pass in is not copied:

def add_item(items):
    items.append("extra")

shopping = ["bread", "milk"]
add_item(shopping)

print(shopping)
['bread', 'milk', 'extra']

The function changed the list that was passed in. Why did a function I called change my data? Because the function received the same list, not a copy. If that is not what you want, make a copy inside the function and work on the copy:

def with_item(items):
    new_items = items.copy()
    new_items.append("extra")
    return new_items

shopping = ["bread", "milk"]
bigger = with_item(shopping)

print(shopping)
print(bigger)
['bread', 'milk']
['bread', 'milk', 'extra']

Do Numbers and Text Have This Problem?

Do numbers and text show the same surprise? Not in the same way. Some values can never be edited after they are created, called immutable values: numbers and strings are examples, so there is nothing to be surprised by:

x = 5
y = x
y = y + 1

print(x, y)
5 6

Adding to y creates a new number and points y at it. The original 5 is never modified. The sharing problem only appears with values you can change in place, such as lists, dictionaries and sets. Even a tuple (a fixed group of values) can fool you: it cannot be edited itself, but a list stored inside a tuple can still be changed, and every name pointing at that tuple sees the change.

Get the Code

Every example in this lesson, with its output, is in a notebook on GitHub: PythonCopyLists.ipynb.

Summary

  • b = a gives one list two names; changing it through either name changes it for both.
  • a is b tells you whether two names point at the same object.
  • a.copy(), list(a) and a[:] create an independent top-level copy.
  • These are shallow copies: nested lists inside are still shared between the original and the copy.
  • copy.deepcopy() copies every level, so nested data becomes fully independent.
  • A list passed to a function is not copied; copy it inside the function if the caller's list must not change.
